paragraphs.heading: A map of life from climate
paragraphs.text: The Holdridge life zones system is a bioclimatic scheme for sorting land areas, and it covers the whole world. Leslie Holdridge first published it in 1947 and updated it in 1967. It is fairly simple, rests on only a few pieces of measured data, and gives objective rules. Its core assumption is that once you know an area's climate, you can map both its soil and its climax vegetation.

paragraphs.heading: From the tropics to the globe
paragraphs.text: Holdridge first built the system for tropical and subtropical regions, but it is now used everywhere. It has been shown to fit Mediterranean and boreal zones as well as tropical ones. It suits cold arid and cold oceanic regions less well, because there moisture takes over as the main factor. It is judged a better fit for tropical vegetation than Merriam's life zones, which lean toward temperate latitudes.

paragraphs.heading: Biotemperature
paragraphs.text: The system puts biotemperature first and does not mainly look at elevation directly. Biotemperature depends on how long the growing season is and how warm it is. To work it out, any temperature below freezing or above 30 °C is set to 0 °C before taking the yearly mean. The reason is that most plants are dormant at those temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Water in and water out
paragraphs.text: Potential evapotranspiration, or PET, is how much water would evaporate and be given off by plants if water were never in short supply. The hotter it is, the higher PET climbs. Evapotranspiration itself, the water that really evaporates from land and is given off by plants, can never exceed it. Dividing precipitation by PET gives the aridity index: below 0.2 means arid or hyperarid, and below 0.5 means dry.

paragraphs.heading: Deserts hot and cold
paragraphs.text: Both cold and warm places can end up dry. In the coldest regions there is too little heat to evaporate much water, so there is little evapotranspiration and little rain, giving polar deserts. In warm regions, hot deserts pair the highest PET with little rain, which dries the soil further. Rain forests, by contrast, combine low PET with the most rain, so rivers carry the surplus water to the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Life zones on the move
paragraphs.text: A major use of the system is to judge how natural vegetation may change as the world warms. Many areas are expected to change life zone type, and more severe change brings bigger shifts over a span that is short by geological standards, leaving people and biomes less time to adjust. Species that cannot adapt would eventually die out. For farming, shifts over just decades mean weather less stable than anything that area has known in human history, and poorer regions are less likely to cope than richer ones.

paragraphs.heading: What it could mean for food
paragraphs.text: One line of research looked at SSP5-8.5, a scenario where greenhouse gas emissions keep rising. Under it, areas producing over half of today's crops and livestock would see very fast life zone shifts. Worldwide, 31% of crop and 34% of livestock production would end up outside a "safe climatic space". Under the low-emissions scenario SSP1-2.6, those shares fall to 5% and 8%.
